title: What is an `ETag` and how do conditional requests work — the server returns an `ETag` (a content hash/version); the client sends `If-None-Match` on a GET to get `304 Not Modified` (saving bandwidth) or `If-Match` on an update to get `412 Precondition Failed` when the resource changed underneath (optimistic concurrency at the HTTP layer)?
shortTitle: What is an ETag and how do conditional requests work

s1_definition.profdef: An ETag, or entity tag, is an opaque identifier the server attaches to a specific version of a resource, usually a hash of the content or a version number. Clients use it in conditional requests. On a GET, the client sends If-None-Match with the ETag it already has, and the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body if unchanged, saving bandwidth. On an update, the client sends If-Match with the ETag it read, and the server returns 412 Precondition Failed if the resource has changed since, giving optimistic concurrency control at the HTTP layer.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh's account statement at National Bank of India has a little version sticker on it, say v7. When his app re-opens the statement, it asks the clerk, I already have v7, has it changed? If not, the clerk says nothing changed, reuse yours, and hands back no paper, saving effort. Now imagine Rajesh edits his profile. He read version v7, fills the form, and submits saying only apply this if it is still v7. If Priya, a joint account holder, already changed it to v8 in the meantime, the clerk refuses and says the record changed underneath you, reload and try again, preventing Rajesh from silently overwriting Priya's change.
s1_definition.oneliner: An ETag is a version tag; If-None-Match on GET gives 304 to save bandwidth, and If-Match on update gives 412 to prevent overwriting a change you did not see.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An ETag, or entity tag, is an opaque identifier the server attaches to a specific version of a resource, usually a hash of the content or a version number. Clients use it in conditional requests. On a GET, the client sends If-None-Match with the ETag it already has, and the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body if unchanged, saving bandwidth. On an update, the client sends If-Match with the ETag it read, and the server returns 412 Precondition Failed if the resource has changed since, giving optimistic concurrency control at the HTTP layer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh's account statement at National Bank of India has a little version sticker on it, say v7. When his app re-opens the statement, it asks the clerk, I already have v7, has it changed? If not, the clerk says nothing changed, reuse yours, and hands back no paper, saving effort. Now imagine Rajesh edits his profile. He read version v7, fills the form, and submits saying only apply this if it is still v7. If Priya, a joint account holder, already changed it to v8 in the meantime, the clerk refuses and says the record changed underneath you, reload and try again, preventing Rajesh from silently overwriting Priya's change.

**One line to remember:** An ETag is a version tag; If-None-Match on GET gives 304 to save bandwidth, and If-Match on update gives 412 to prevent overwriting a change you did not see.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh's mobile app at National Bank of India re-fetches his account every few seconds to keep the balance fresh, each time downloading the full account payload even when nothing changed, wasting mobile data. This is exactly what conditional GET with ETags fixes. The app sends If-None-Match with the ETag it already has, and when nothing changed the server returns a tiny 304 with no body.

Problem 2 — Rajesh and Priya share a joint current account. Both open the profile editor showing version 7. Rajesh changes the address and saves. Priya, still on version 7, changes the phone and saves, silently wiping out Rajesh's address change. This is the lost update problem, and it is exactly what If-Match with 412 prevents. Priya's save carries If-Match v7, but the current version is now v8, so the server returns 412 and tells her to reload.

Problem 3 — The bank wants this concurrency safety to line up with the database. By using a JPA version column, the same version that drives the ETag also drives database optimistic locking, so the two layers agree.

We will build an account service that returns an ETag on GET, honours If-None-Match to return 304, and honours If-Match on update to return 412 on conflict. The demo shows a repeated GET getting a 304 and two concurrent edits where the second gets a 412.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/etag-account-service-1.0.0.jar

# First GET → 200 with ETag "1"
curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/CUR3001

# Conditional GET with If-None-Match "1" → 304 Not Modified (no body)
curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/CUR3001 -H 'If-None-Match: "1"'

# Rajesh updates phone with If-Match "1" → 200 + new ETag "2"
curl -i -X PUT http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/CUR3001 \
  -H 'If-Match: "1"' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"phone":"8887776666"}'

# Priya updates with STALE If-Match "1" (now version 2) → 412 Precondition Failed
curl -i -X PUT http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/CUR3001 \
  -H 'If-Match: "1"' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"phone":"1112223333"}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the joint account CUR3001 starts at version 1. The app does a GET, then a conditional GET, then Rajesh updates, then Priya updates with a stale ETag.

Step 1: The first GET returns 200 with the full account and an ETag of "1". The app stores this ETag.

Step 2: A few seconds later the app sends a conditional GET with If-None-Match "1". The current version is still 1, so the ETags match, and the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body. The app reuses its cached account, saving the full payload download.

Step 3: Rajesh opens the editor, having read version 1, and submits a phone change with If-Match "1". The current version is still 1, so the precondition passes. The service updates the phone and bumps the version to 2. The response is 200 with a new ETag "2".

Step 4: Priya, who also read version 1 earlier, now submits her phone change with a stale If-Match "1". The current version is now 2, so the precondition fails. The server returns 412 Precondition Failed and does not apply her change. Rajesh's address change is safe.

Step 5: Priya's app, seeing the 412, reloads the account, gets version 2 and ETag "2", and can reapply her change on top of the latest version. No update was silently lost, which is the whole point of optimistic concurrency.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 22:25:00 INFO  GET  /accounts/CUR3001                -> 200 ETag:"1"
2026-10-25 22:25:03 INFO  GET  /accounts/CUR3001 If-None-Match:"1" -> 304 Not Modified (no body)
2026-10-25 22:25:05 INFO  PUT  /accounts/CUR3001 If-Match:"1"   -> 200 ETag:"2" (Rajesh, phone updated)
2026-10-25 22:25:06 WARN  PUT  /accounts/CUR3001 If-Match:"1"   -> 412 Precondition Failed (Priya, stale)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── Conditional GET (bandwidth) ────────────────────
  App (has ETag "1") → GET If-None-Match:"1"
    │
    ▼
  AccountController.get()
    │ current version = 1 → etag "1" == If-None-Match ?  YES
    ▼
  304 Not Modified (NO body) → app reuses cached copy

  ── Conditional UPDATE (concurrency) ───────────────
  Rajesh read v1 → PUT If-Match:"1"  {phone:8887776666}
    │ current etag "1" == "1" ? YES → update → version 2
    ▼
  200 OK ETag:"2"

  Priya read v1 (stale) → PUT If-Match:"1"  {phone:1112223333}
    │ current etag "2" == "1" ? NO
    ▼
  412 Precondition Failed → Priya reloads (gets v2) → reapplies
  (Rajesh's change is NOT silently overwritten)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — ETag + Conditional Requests ═══

  ┌─ Semantics ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ETag = opaque version tag (quotes are syntax)          │
  │  GET + If-None-Match match   → 304 (no body)            │
  │  GET + If-None-Match differ  → 200 + body + new ETag    │
  │  PUT + If-Match match        → apply, bump version      │
  │  PUT + If-Match differ       → 412 Precondition Failed  │
  │  client treats ETag as OPAQUE (echo only, never parse)  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │      AccountController        │
  │  - etagOf(a): "version"       │
  │  + get(id, If-None-Match)     │ 200/304
  │  + update(id, If-Match, body) │ 200/412
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ uses
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │        AccountService         │
  │  + find(id): Account          │
  │  + update(id,u): bumpVersion  │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: version ──────────────────
  [v1] ─GET─→ 200 ETag "1"
  [v1] ─GET If-None-Match "1"─→ 304
  [v1] ─PUT If-Match "1"─→ [v2] 200 ETag "2"
  [v2] ─PUT If-Match "1" (stale)─→ 412 (no change)

  ── Call Chain (stale update) ───────────────
  1. PUT If-Match:"1" ; current version 2
  2.   → etagOf == "2" ; "2" != "1"
  3.   → 412 Precondition Failed (lost update prevented)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An ETag, or entity tag, is an opaque identifier the server attaches to a specific version of a resource, usually a content hash or a version number, returned in the ETag header. It powers conditional requests in two directions. On a read, the client stores the ETag and sends If-None-Match on the next GET, and if the resource is unchanged the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body, so the client reuses its cached copy and saves bandwidth. On a write, the client sends If-Match with the ETag it read, and if the resource changed since then the server returns 412 Precondition Failed and rejects the update.

The read side is a performance win. In my work at National Bank of India, Rajesh's app re-fetched his account every few seconds to keep the balance fresh, and without ETags it downloaded the full payload each time. With conditional GET, when nothing changed the server returned a tiny 304, which on a mobile connection is a real data saving, and a CDN in front can serve that 304 even more cheaply.

The write side is a correctness win, because it gives optimistic concurrency at the HTTP layer and solves the lost update problem. Rajesh and Priya share a joint account, and both opened the editor on version 7. Rajesh saved an address change, bumping it to version 8. When Priya saved her phone change with If-Match version 7, the server saw the current version was 8 and returned 412, so her stale write was rejected instead of silently overwriting Rajesh's change. Her app then reloaded version 8 and reapplied her edit on top, so no change was lost.

The nuances I always mention are that the ETag is opaque, so the client must only echo it back and never parse it, and that it should change whenever the resource meaningfully changes. In practice I back it with a JPA version column, so the same version that produces the ETag also drives database optimistic locking, and the HTTP layer and the database layer agree about concurrency. That combination of cheap revalidation and safe concurrent updates is exactly why ETags are so valuable in a banking API where both bandwidth and never losing a customer's change matter.

---

keyPoints: ETag: version identifier for a resource — cache validation
If-None-Match: client sends ETag, server returns 304 if unchanged
Saves bandwidth and reduces server load
